claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain in tungsten-based plasma-facing materials is chiefly governed by intrinsic grain-boundary stability.
High-temperature toughness in tungsten-based plasma-facing materials is chiefly governed by intrinsic grain-boundary stability.
The tendency to form embrittling grain-boundary precipitates is the relevant aspect of grain-boundary stability.
Grain boundaries with minimal precipitation accommodate plastic deformation more effectively than compromised boundaries.
Grain boundaries with minimal precipitation retain greater toughness than compromised boundaries.
Conventionally produced polycrystalline tungsten-based alloys contain impurities capable of precipitating during high-temperature exposure.
Tailored thermal annealing can stabilize grain boundaries without changing the alloy's overall composition.
Slow cooling promotes grain-boundary stability relative to standard fast cooling.
The proposed mechanism applies in the approximately 1200°C to 1600°C operational regime.
At operational fusion temperatures, unstable grain boundaries permit impurity segregation and nucleation of secondary phases.
Impurity phases formed at grain boundaries embrittle the boundary region.
Grain-boundary embrittlement reduces cohesive strength across grains.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesive strength increases plastic strain under load.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesive strength decreases toughness.
Stabilized grain boundaries prevent or limit formation of detrimental secondary phases.
Limiting detrimental grain-boundary phases produces a more uniform distribution of plastic deformation.
Grain-boundary-stabilized samples should exhibit lower high-temperature plastic strain than conventionally processed controls.
Grain-boundary-stabilized samples should exhibit greater toughness than conventionally processed controls.
Outside the stated temperature regime or at different energy-deposition scales, bulk dislocation plasticity may govern behavior instead.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says stable boundaries accommodate plastic deformation more effectively, which can imply greater plastic deformability, whereas the mechanism assigns increased plastic strain to unstable, embrittled boundaries and the prediction expects stabilization to reduce plastic strain. The intended meaning of plastic strain—beneficial ductility versus excessive deformation under a fixed load—is not resolved.
